extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, physicists, and astronomers (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and states mathematical propositions, hypotheses, and scholia concerning motion of fluids, propagation of light and sound, vortices, and laws of planetary motion (Book III) as presented in Newton's Principia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. L. Prob. XIII — Invenire pulsuum distantias
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporis, cujus tremore pulsus excitantur, inveniatur numerus Vibrationum dato tempore. Per numerum illum dividatur spatium quod pulsus eodem tempore percurrere possit, & pars inventa erit pulsus unius latitudo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: measure number of vibrations of the body in a given time; determine the distance a pulse travels in the same time; divide that distance by the vibration-count to obtain the width (wavelength) of one pulse. (Q.E.I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium — Light propagates rectilinearly; sound consists of air-pulses
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectant Propositiones novissimæ ad motum Lucis & Sonorum. Lux enim cum propagetur secundum lineas rectas, in actione sola consistere nequit. Soni vero propterea quod a corporibus tremulis oriuntur, nihil aliud sunt quàm aeris pulsus propagati.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and evidence: Light's rectilinear propagation follows from prior propositions (XLI & XLII). Sound follows from vibrations of bodies and is manifested by tremors induced in objects (e.g., tympanum). Faster/shorter tremors are harder to excite. Observational support: pendulum/organ-pipe measurements and calculated pulse distances concordant with experiments (Mersennus, Robervallus), and echo/pendulum experiments give bounds for sound speed and pulse spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical method for pulse/wavelength estimation from organ pipes and vibrating strings
rubrics_metrics.description: From observations (Mersennus): a tense string giving unison with an organ pipe shows ~104 vibrations per second; the sound in one second describes a certain number of feet, giving pulse spacing ~9¼ feet (about double pipe length).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use published experiments (string/pipe unison counts) and speed of sound calculations to estimate inter-pulse distances; infer that pulse widths in open pipes are roughly twice the pipe length. Compare multiple observers and experiments to bracket likely pulse wavelengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of reduced air density on sound (evacuated vessels)
rubrics_metrics.description: In vessels where the air is greatly evacuated, sounds are notably diminished; e.g., if one hundredth part of air remains, sound will be diminished one-hundredfold and will be as if the source were ten times farther away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test: compare two equally sounding bodies, one in an evacuated vessel and one in free air, placed at distances in inverse ratio of air densities; if prior body's sound does not exceed the latter's, the hypothesis about air-mediated sound propagation holds. Note: complete evacuation is practically difficult; even small remaining air significantly affects audibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of echoes and amplification in tubes (stenterophonic effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounds in long galleries produce multiple echoes; motion in tubes that hinder dilation loses its energy more slowly and recurs more strongly, so repeated impulses augment motion and thus amplify sound in tubes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: reciprocal motion tends to increase with each return when the medium limits expansion; this explains why tubes can strengthen certain sounds (as observed) and why echoes correspond to pendulum oscillations induced by sound recurrences. Use pendulum timing to relate echo recurrence and tube amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (Sect. IX) — Resistance proportional to separation-velocity (lack of lubricity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resistentiam, quæ oritur ex defectu lubricitatis partium Fluidi, cæteris paribus, proportionalem esse velocitati, qua partes Fluidi separantur ab invicem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hypothesis posits that, all else equal, the resistance arising from imperfect lubrication of fluid parts is proportional to the velocity at which parts separate. It is used as an assumption to derive further theoretical results about vortical motion; Newton notes that in some situations resistance may grow slower than velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LI (Theor. XXXVIII) — Cylindrical vortex: periodic times ∝ distance from axis
rubrics_metrics.description: If an infinitely long solid cylinder rotates uniformly about its axis in a homogeneous infinite fluid and agitates the fluid into circular motion with each fluid part preserving uniform motion, then the periodic times of fluid parts are proportional to their distances from the cylinder axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration constructs concentric cylindrical shells as solids and reasons by mutual pressures (per the hypothesis of resistance proportionality) producing translations inversely proportional to surfaces, yielding angular-motion differentials proportional to inverse-squares leading to periodic times proportional to radial distance. Corollaries: angular motions of fluid particles are reciprocal to their distances from axis; absolute velocities equal; adding/removing a common angular motion doesn't change relative motions; propagation and retardation behaviors in bounded cylinders follow the same proportionalities. Practical note: these conclusions are testable in deep stationary water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LII (Theor. XXXIX) — Spherical vortex: periodic times ∝ square of distance from center
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid sphere rotates uniformly about its axis in a homogeneous infinite fluid and agitates the fluid into circular motion with each fluid part preserving uniform motion, then the periodic times of fluid parts are proportional to the squares of their distances from the sphere's center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument parallels the cylindrical case but with concentric spherical shells; mutual pressures give translations inversely proportional to surface areas (∝ 1/r^2), leading to angular motion differentials proportional to inverse-cubes and hence periodic times ∝ r^2. Corollaries: angular motions reciprocally ∝ r^2, absolute velocities reciprocally ∝ r (applied squares), propagation of motion through fluid, necessity of an active principle to maintain vortices against loss, behavior in bounded vessels (matching periodic times to shell radii), and implications about conservation/transfer of motion across shells. Scholium discusses implications for planetary vortices and notes that observed planetary laws (Kepler's) do not match the r^2 scaling without additional, implausible assumptions about varying fluid properties or resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to spherical vortex proposition (consequences for vortices and conservation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple corollaries: (1) angular motions of fluid parts about globe ∝ reciprocal squares of distances; (2) motion will propagate in vortex fashion through fluid; (3) interior parts transmit their motion outward preserving momentum; (4) to maintain a vortex indefinitely, an active principle must supply motion to the central body equal to what it imparts to the vortex; (5–11) further corollaries about interaction of multiple rotating bodies, propagation in enclosed vessels, and steady states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These corollaries enumerate dynamical consequences: vortices transfer motion outward and would, absent continual input, decay; multiple rotating bodies produce combined vortices; enclosures and vessels alter but do not prevent the propagation of vortex motion; comparison to astronomical observations is discussed (see scholium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium — Vortices cannot account for planetary motion (conflict with Kepler's law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The periodic times of parts of a vortex produced by rotating matter scale as the square (or higher) of the distance from the center, whereas planetary periods obey Kepler's sesquialteral (3/2 power) relation; to reconcile requires implausible assumptions about decreasing fluid density with radius or resistance increasing faster than velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton argues that observed planetary periods (Kepler's third law) conflict with the r^2 (or greater) dependence derived for vortices; only by assuming additional ad hoc properties of the medium could vortices match observation, so philosophers should consider that vortices as ordinarily conceived are incompatible with astronomical phenomena. He invites others to show how the sesquialteral law could be reconciled by different fluid properties, but regards such reconciliations as unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIII (Theor. XL) — Density criterion for bodies returning to same vortex orbit
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies carried in a vortex that return to the same orbit have the same density as the vortex; such bodies move according to the same law as the parts of the vortex (with respect to velocity and trajectory determination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: freeze a small part of the vortex (so it becomes solid) and note it would continue moving the same way; conversely, if a solid with different density were placed, it would move differently (spiral inward if rarer, outward if denser). Corollaries: a solid that always returns to the same orbit relatively rests in the surrounding fluid; if vortex density is uniform, a body can revolve at any given radial distance; this result is used to argue planets cannot be carried by material vortices if they do not match the vortex density distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on vortices vs planetary motion (illustrative contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton demonstrates contradictions between vortex dynamics and observed planetary motions (e.g., Jovian satellite distances & periods, apparent motion of the Sun's diurnal motion if Earth moved with surrounding medium's varying velocity), concluding vortex hypothesis conflicts with astronomical phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He uses observational tables (satellites' periods and semidiameters) to show the vortex-derived scaling does not fit actual satellite data, and offers a qualitative argument that vortices would predict different apparent diurnal solar motion than observed. Concludes vortices disturb rather than explain celestial motions; refers reader to Book I for alternative explanation in free space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis I (Book III) — Economy of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Causas rerum naturalium non plures admitti debere, quàm quæ & vera sint & earum Phænomenis explicandis sufficiunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological principle (Occam-like): admit no more natural causes than are true and that suffice to explain phenomena. Used as a meta-principle for selecting theories and hypotheses in physical science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis II — Same causes produce same kinds of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideoque effectuum naturalium ejusdem generis eædem sunt causæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological claim: similar phenomena (e.g., respiration in man and beast) should be explained by the same causes; supports generalization and unification across natural kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis III — Transformability of bodies and continuity of qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus omne in alterius cujuscunque generis corpus transformari posse, & qualitatum gradus omnes intermedios sucessivè induere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts matter can change form between kinds and qualities admit continuous gradations; a premise permitting continuum-like transitions in explanations of natural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis IV — Rest of the world's center
rubrics_metrics.description: Centrum Systematis Mundani quiescere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stipulation about the reference frame: the center of the world-system is taken as at rest for subsequent reasoning; Newton notes different authors may take different centers (Earth vs Sun) but adopts a center for theoretical economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis V — Kepler's third law for Jovian satellites
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas circumjoviales, radiis ad centrum Jovis ductis, areas describere temporibus proportionales, eorumque tempora periodica esse in ratione sesquialtera distantiarum ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical premise based on observations of Jovian satellites: areas swept about Jupiter are proportional to times and periods scale as the 3/2 power of their mean distances. Newton cites Flamsteed's micrometric and eclipse-based measures confirming this relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis VI — Primary planets revolve about the Sun
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas quinque primarios Mercurium, Venerem, Martem, Jovem & Saturnum Orbibus suis Solem cingere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of heliocentrism for the five primary planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) supported by observational phases and other evidence; used as a working assumption to derive gravitational laws for the solar system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis VII — Kepler's third law for the primary planets and Earth
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetarum quinque primariorum, & (vel Solis circa Terram vel) Terræ circa Solem tempora periodica esse in ratione sesquialtera mediocrium distantiarum à Sole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopts Kepler's law (period ∝ distance^(3/2)) as a foundational empirical law for primary planets and Earth; Newton notes good agreement between distances derived from periods and those measured by Kepler/Bullialdus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis VIII — Area law with respect to Sun; apparent motions with respect to Earth
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetarum primariorum radiis ad Terram ductis areas describere temporibus minimè proportionales; at radiis ad Solem ductis areas temporibus proportionales percurrere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes apparent complex motions when viewed from Earth (retrograde, stationary) from true heliocentric motion which obeys the area law precisely; supports using heliocentric frame for simpler laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis IX — Lunar area law about Earth's center
rubrics_metrics.description: Lunam radio ad centrum terræ ducto aream tempori proportionalem describere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts the Moon sweeps out areas about Earth's center proportional to time; acknowledges small solar perturbations but treats them as negligible for present hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. I (Theor. I, Book III) — Forces on planets about Jupiter directed to Jupiter ∝ 1/r^2
rubrics_metrics.description: Vires, quibus Planetæ circumjoviales perpetuo retrahuntur à motibus rectilineis & in orbibus suis retinentur, respicere centrum Jovis, & esse reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum locorum ab eodem centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical basis: follows from Hypothesis V and prior propositions in Book I (and II/III references). Establishes that the central attracting force acting on Jovian satellites is directed to Jupiter's center and varies inversely as the square of the distance. Used as a specific application of inverse-square attraction to satellite motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II (Theor. II, Book III) — Forces on planets directed to Sun ∝ 1/r^2
rubrics_metrics.description: Vires, quibus Planetæ primarii perpetuo retrahuntur à motibus rectilineis, & in Orbibus suis retinentur, respicere Solem, & esse reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation uses Hypothesis VIII and Book I propositions; the posterior part is reinforced by Kepler's third law for planetary periods. Newton notes that small deviations would have large observable consequences (e.g., apsidal motion), so inverse-square dependence is strongly supported by astronomical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III (Theor. III, Book III) — Lunar centripetal force toward Earth ∝ 1/r^2
rubrics_metrics.description: Vim qua Luna retinetur in Orbe suo respicere terram, & esse reciprocò ut quadratum distantiæ locorum ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument references Hypothesis IX and motions of lunar apogee (very slow) to argue that the force retaining the Moon toward Earth is effectively inverse-square with distance. Newton acknowledges small corrections from the Sun but finds the inverse-square relation the accurate leading behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IV (Theor. IV, Book III) — Moon gravitates to the Earth and is retained by gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lunam gravitare in terram, & vi gravitatis retrahi semper à motu rectilineo, & in orbe suo retineri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses measured lunar distance (various astronomers' values discussed) and prior theoretical results to state that the Moon is attracted to Earth by gravity which keeps it in orbit. Newton discusses observational estimates of lunar distance and parallax corrections; this proposition ties gravitational theory to observed lunar motion.
